data.title: Thailand urges Cambodia not to internationalise land border dispute
data.author: eng editor 3
data.summary:
Thailand urges Cambodia not to internationalise land border dispute
Thailand has urged Cambodia not to internationalise the land border dispute, saying that it deeply regretted that Cambodia used the Francophonie and ASEAN summits to vilify Thailand. The remarks came amid an ongoing process to resolve the two countries’ maritime dispute through UN’s conciliation.
Speaking on 15 November at the Francophonie Summit’s opening in Phnom Penh, Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet said that Thai troops still occupy parts of Cambodian territory after last year’s deadly border fighting, according to Camboja.
He said that about 20,000 Cambodians remain unable to return home, calling for existing agreements to be honoured and for joint border demarcation to resume. Hun Manet was also reported as saying that Cambodia did not initiate either of the two rounds of armed clashes with Thailand in 2025, adding that no borders had been altered through the use of armed force or the creation of faits accomplis.
In addition, the Cambodian representative at the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila delivered a similar message on the same day.
In response to the remark made by his Cambodian counterpart, PM Anutin Charnvirakul said that Thailand remained committed to resolving the differences peacefully through bilateral mechanisms and in accordance with international law.
He asserted that both Cambodia and Thailand must avoid internationalising all bilateral issues and should “advocate confidence-building measures with each other” if each side desires to restore friendship.
The Thai Foreign Ministry also issued an official statement expressing regret that Cambodia used its position as host of the meeting to highlight throughout the programme a number of unfounded allegations deliberately meant to vilify Thailand, particularly the claim that that Thailand occupies Cambodian territory and prevents approximately 20,000 Cambodian nationals from returning to their homes.

data.title: Bangkok’s EV Motorcycle Taxis Shoulder the Battery Burden
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Bangkok’s EV Motorcycle Taxis Shoulder the Battery Burden
When Samart Dornburan heads out to work as a motorcycle taxi driver, he takes four batteries with him. He uses three during the day and saves the fourth for the journey home. Each battery gives him a range of around 40–50 kilometres. If he runs out of power on the road, he has to pay someone to deliver a replacement.
“I’d earn 100 baht from fares, and 50 baht would go on paying someone to bring me a battery,” he recalled.
Samart has driven motorcycle taxis for more than 30 years and now heads the Bang Kruai Samakkhi motorcycle taxi stand in Nonthaburi province. He switched to an electric motorcycle during a pilot project that provided a shared battery-swapping station. But when the project ended, the station and spare batteries were taken away. He then began carrying his own batteries. Some fellow drivers sold their electric motorcycles, and Samart bought their vehicles and batteries to keep using them.
Samart Dornburan, head of the Bang Kruai Samakkhi motorcycle taxi stand, has driven motorcycle taxis for more than 30 years. He began using an electric motorcycle during a pilot project.
Lower costs, but when the motorcycle stops, so does the income A major convenience store in Bangkok uses plug-in electric motorcycles for deliveries. (Photo by Pattaraporn Phongamphai)

Figures presented to the Bangkok Metropolitan Council in early 2026 show that the city has around 5,488 authorised motorcycle taxi stands and more than 61,000 approved motorcycles. Meanwhile, the Thai–German Cooperation on Energy, Mobility and Climate project (TGC-EMC) estimates that Bangkok’s petrol-powered motorcycle taxis emit around 80,000–100,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide and approximately 16 tonnes of PM2.5 annually.

data.title: Myanmar migrant leader arrested over his birth record, denied bail
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Myanmar migrant leader arrested over his birth record, denied bail
Weera Saengthong, a leader of the Myanmar migrant network Bright Future who has been protesting Myanmar-run CI centers in Thailand, has been arrested and detained without bail over allegations that he used false evidence to obtain a Thai birth certificate.
Weera, also known as Suraj Giri, turned himself into the police in Kanchanaburi on 13 November. An arrest warrant was issued for him on 9 November after the Sai Yok District Registration Office revoked his birth certificate.
Registration officials said that five witnesses who supported his birth registration gave statements in 2010 that did not match, that checks found inconsistencies in his stated place of birth and date of entry, and that he did not produce further evidence within the 30 days he was given.
Democratic Voice of Burma (DVB) reported that Weera has been denied bail and remains in detention.
Local media reported that Songchai Niamhom, member of the ultra-royalist King Protection Group, filed a complaint with the Ministry of Interior claiming that Weera used false evidence to obtain a Thai birth certificate and an ID card known as the “Number 0 card” issued for unregistered individuals, stateless persons, or members of ethnic communities.
Weera was assaulted on 1 November by members of ultra-royalist groups during a protest staged by the Bright Future network calling for the abolition of Myanmar-run Certificate of Identity (CI) centres in Thailand and for the Thai-issued “pink card” to be accepted as workers’ only identity document as they see the CI centres as a way for the Myanmar regime to exploit workers.
At about 11.30am, members of two royalist groups confronted Weera: the People’s Centre for the Protection of the Monarchy, led by Anon Klinkaew, and the King Protection Group, led by Songchai Niamhom. data.title: Supreme Court sentences 29-year-old activist to prison over FB post
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Supreme Court sentences 29-year-old activist to prison over FB post
The Supreme Court today (19 November) sentenced activist Pimchanok Jirataiyanon, 29, to 2 years in prison on a royal defamation charge over a Facebook post made in 2022.
The post in question said “The government is shit, the institution is shit,” which a complainant interpreted as intended to refer to the royal institution without mentioning it explicitly.
The activist was apprehended at her residence in Bangkok on 18 March 2022, without having received a prior summons.
She testified that she did not refer to the royal institution as accused, but rather an educational institution. In addition, she argued that the royal defamation law covers only the King, the Queen, the Heir Apparent, and the Regent, rather than the whole royal institution.
In September 2023, the Chiang Mai Provincial Court found her guilty on the grounds that despite not mentioning any specific monarch, the royal defamation law protects the monarchy as an institution. She was sentenced to 3 years in prison, reduced to 2 years because she gave useful testimony. In April 2025, the Appeal Court upheld the ruling.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) said today (19 November) that the Supreme Court upheld the verdict, finding her guilty on the grounds that the royal defamation law exists not only to protect the reputation of the King, the Queen, the Heir Apparent, and the Regent, but also to protect national security and to protect the King as the head of state and one of the country’s main institutions. It noted that Pimchanok is an activist who has participated in “anti-monarchy” activities, as well as participated in protests demanding the repeal of the royal defamation law and the release of political prisoners, and so it believes the post refers to the monarchy.
Pimchanok is serving her sentence at the Chiang Mai Women Correctional Institution. Her detention brings the number of people detained on royal defamation charges to 35.

data.title: UN Special Rapporteur calls for revise or repeal of royal defamation law following sentencing of Anon Nampa
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
UN Special Rapporteur calls for revise or repeal of royal defamation law following sentencing of Anon Nampa
Andrea Bolaños Vargas, the UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of Human Rights Defenders, has called for Thailand to impose an immediate moratorium on prosecutions and imprisonments under the royal defamation law - Section 112 of the Thai Criminal Code - and for the revise or repeal of the law to bring it in line with international human rights standards.
The call came after the Criminal Court on 30 October sentenced human rights lawyer Anon Nampa to 2 years and 8 months on a royal defamation charge over a speech delivered at a protest on 25 November 2020. On 12 November, the Appeal Court sentenced him to 4 years in prison on royal defamation and computer crimes charges for 3 Facebook posts which called for monarchy reform and criticized the use of the royal defamation law against critics of the monarchy.
Anon is now facing a cumulative prison sentence of 34 years and 5 months.
Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer in Thailand, has been in prison for more than three years. On 30 October, the Criminal Court sentenced him to another two years and eight months for speaking at a peaceful assembly. He was convicted under Thailand’s lèse-majesté law, which criminalises defaming, insulting or threatening the King, Queen, heir apparent or regent.
On 12 November, the Court of Appeal upheld another conviction against him under Section 112 of the Criminal Code and the Computer Crime Act, confirming a further four-year prison sentence. The case relates to three Facebook posts he published in January 2021 concerning the enforcement of Section 112 and monarchy reforms.
His cumulative prison sentence remains at 34 years, five months and 20 days. If he serves the full sentence, he will be in his 70s when he is released. No one should lose decades of their life for speaking out peacefully.

data.title: “Gen Z protest” takes to the street for education reform, new Constitution
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
“Gen Z protest” takes to the street for education reform, new Constitution
On Friday afternoon (20 November), a student-led protest took place by the Democracy Monument on Ratchadamnoen Road to call for education reform, public participation for young people, and a new Constitution.
Organised by activist groups Studem Network and Free Thai Youth, the protest started at 15.00 on the foothpath in front of Satriwithaya School, later moving into the street and closing half of the roundabout around the Democracy Monument. Participants took turns giving speeches about social and political issues, including authoritarianism in schools, abolition of compulsory military service, labour rights, pollution, and constitutional amendments.
One Mathayom 6 (Year 12) student joined the protest with a placard saying “There’s poison in our rivers.” She said she wanted to call attention to heavy metal contamination in several rivers resulting from mines in Myanmar. The contamination affects people’s way of life, she said, but the government has not found a solution.
“Instead, the government tells the people not to use the water, not to use the water for drinking, not to use it to water plants, which is not possible. It’s not practical. It’s a bit irresponsible to say these things,” she said.
She also said she wants to call attention to Chinese-funded waste processing plants opened around 9 years ago after an order was issued by the NCPO allowing them to open near communities. She said her main demands for the government are about the environment, because young people will have to live with these conditions for a long time.
“Are you really going to leave us with a country like this? The environment is no good,” she said.

data.title: Appeal Court sentences opposition MP to prison for royal defamation over social media posts
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Appeal Court sentences opposition MP to prison for royal defamation over social media posts
The Appeal Court today (23 November) sentenced Rukchanok Srinork, an MP from the opposition People’s Party to 3 years in prison on a royal defamation charge for two tweets from 2021 about a COVID-19 vaccine monopoly and the monarchy.
Rukchanok faced two charges over the tweets in July and October 2021. The complaint was filed with the Technology Crime Suppression Division by Manirat Laowaloet, requesting legal action against Rukchanok, who was then a member of the Clubhouse for Democracy.
According to Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR), Rukchanok's first message criticized the government’s decision to grant a licence to produce the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine to only one company, which caused a vaccine shortage affecting the lives of people. She also attached her picture standing next to the image of King Vajiralongkorn and holding a banner that read “Tyrant (noun); Ruler of the country who uses their power to cause suffering to those under their rule.”
In the second message, Rukchanok reposted a message from a Twitter (now X) account expressing dissatisfaction towards the King, which stated that “the people will not be free until the feudalist (sakdina) group has been eliminated.” The user she reposted from was quoting a tweet from another Twitter user containing a protest sign from a 16 October 2020 protest.
In December 2023, the Criminal Court sentenced her to 6 years in prison on royal defamation and computer crimes charges. TLHR said today (23 November) that the Appeal Court revised her sentence to 3 years in prison on a royal defamation charge for the tweet about vaccine monopoly, dismissing the computer crime charge. The Appeal Court also dismissed charges relating to the second post as it has some doubts regarding evidence presented by the prosecution.

data.title: Three-finger salute raised high, broad and multifaceted in Indonesia
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Three-finger salute raised high, broad and multifaceted in Indonesia
Article first published in The Jakarta Post
In the early morning on Oct. 28, as students, labor groups and civic activists gathered in Jakarta and other Indonesian cities to protest a series of government policies and inaction under the hashtag #IndonesiaSadar (Indonesia aware), social media feeds swelled with three-finger salutes in diverse colors, formats and artistic interpretations. In adopting this gesture, Indonesian demonstrators drew upon imagery from pro-democracy movements across Asia.
Originally popularized by the movie The Hunger Games as a silent expression of defiance by the oppressed citizens of Panem, the three-finger salute was first adopted by student protesters in Thailand following the 2014 military coup and later that year, by demonstrators in Hong Kong during the Umbrella Movement.
The gesture resurfaced in subsequent protest waves across both jurisdictions: in Hong Kong during the 2019-2020 demonstrations as a symbol of resistance against Beijing-backed authorities and in Thailand during the 2020-2021 protests against the military-dominated government. In Thailand, it was also imbued with the French revolutionary ideals of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity, loosely translated as "No coup, liberty, democracy".
This cross-fertilization of iconography was cultivated by youth-led activist networks across Hong Kong, Taiwan and Thailand under the digital banner of the Milk Tea Alliance, a coalition united by a regional beverage culture and a shared commitment to resisting authoritarianism. The alliance subsequently expanded to Myanmar and other Southeast Asian nations, bringing its political ideals and visual vocabulary along. It was in Myanmar, in fact, that the salute achieved its most potent visual impact in the uprising against the February 2021 coup, as three-finger memes, political cartoons, and digital graphics proliferated far beyond street rallies. data.title: Former PM Thaksin challenges asset seizure in 17-billion baht Shin Corp tax dispute
data.author: eng editor 3
data.summary:
Former PM Thaksin challenges asset seizure in 17-billion baht Shin Corp tax dispute
The Central Tax Court has dismissed former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra’s request for a temporary injunction to suspend the Revenue Department’s seizure of over 17 billion baht. This is the latest development in a long-running Shin Corporation tax dispute against the former PM dating back to 2006.
After a dispute of nearly 20 years including 10 years in court, the Supreme Court in 2025 ordered the former PM to pay back taxes amounting 17 billion baht related to the 2006 sales of shares in his telecom company Shin Corporation, known as Shin Corp.
On 2 July, Thaksin filed a lawsuit with the Central Tax Court against the Revenue Department, arguing that the income arising from the share sale had already been taxed. The former PM also filed a temporary injunction to suspend the asset seizure.
However, on 16 November, the request for temporary injunction was dismissed, while the preliminary hearing is expected to take place on 21 December.
The Shin Corporation tax saga The case stems from the sale of shares in Thaksin’s telecoms firm Shin Corporation on 23 January 2006, which generated a 73-billion-baht windfall for the Shinawatra family. At the time, the shares were sold to Singapore-based state-owned investment company Temasek Holdings.
In 1999, Thaksin also established another company, Ample Rich, in which he was the only shareholder. He transferred Shin Corporation shares to Ample Rich. Thaksin’s children, Pintongta and Panthongtae, later became the company’s shareholders and directors in 2005.
The controversy arose from the sale of shares that Ample Rich had held since 1999 to Pintongta and Panthongtae for only 1 baht per share.
On 23 January 2006, Pintongta and Panthongtae sold the shares for 49 baht per share, generating a profit of approximately 15 billion baht.
